note:
v1, TAKE UP THE SLACK (track fifteen, drawn empty: the song I wanted to make; whole-song skeleton, 3:55). A HAULING SONG. A crew hauls in four at 92: the shantyman calls (two bars), the crew answers "Take up the slack" (the third), and on the fourth bar's downbeat everybody pulls: "Haul!". The band's riff is not in four. THE IDEA, in one place: at 0:13 the riff is fifteen sixteenths long, so its head (the one open chord) falls after the crew's pull by three beats (0:21), then two (0:31), then one (0:42), and on the fourth pull (0:52) it lands with them. The slack is taken up, and the chorus at 0:55 is in four, band and crew together: common time as something arrived at.
LISTEN FOR: 0:03 the first call, voices and stomps only. 0:13 the first verse, the riff creeping toward the pull. 0:55 "Haul away, haul away home". 1:16 the second verse: the riff is seventeen now (the tritone added) and the rope pays out the other way, 3, 7, 11, 15 sixteenths after the pulls; at 1:57 he calls "Hold fast" for one bar more and it lands on the chorus (2:00). 2:21 'easy': quiet, two clean guitars turning the fifteen against the seventeen. 2:42 the third verse: the left guitar has the fifteen and the right the seventeen; at the first pull (2:50) the right hand is a beat early and the left a beat late ("a man too soon and a man too late"), and at the second (3:00) they meet. 3:03 the chorus twice, with the second pair of guitars and a second gang a fourth over the pulls. 3:44 voices and stomps again: "and make her fast".
THE SOUND: the album's own (the twin and wall guitars, bass and kit as Common Measure sets them, which reads within 2 dB of the records), and two voices of the engine I built: the shantyman on the plain sung voice and a crew of five, both with the newest diction and with effort in the tone (a shout is brighter).
THE WORDS WERE CHOSEN BY A RECOGNISER, the one ear I have (each voice alone, small.en). First draft, on the library's old man: half the shantyman's words read, and the song's key word never did: 'hand' came back as 'end', 'and' or 'N' on four voices, where 'man' in the same line read 9 of 9. So the sung word is 'man' and the hands are the guitarists'. 'The tide is high and the hour is soon' read as 'all that I desire' on every voice and was rewritten from words that had read. The old man's rasp and breath cost words, so the shantyman is the plain voice. 'Haul' with the dictionary's vowel read 'home' or 'hole' 14 times in 14; with AA the crew's shout reads 'haul' or 'hall'. AS IT STANDS: the verses' calls read 65% (77 of 119 words, six of eleven lines at 7 or more of 9-10), the crew's answers 37 of 51; the CHORUS does not read ('haul away' comes back 'home, away', once 'hallelujah'): the long H-word over five singers is the engine's weak consonant, and that is a bead, not a mix move.
MEASURED (seeds 0/11): 98.568 / 98.634; -10.0 LUFS, -1.29 dBTP. Finished, by section: first call -13.5, verses -11.0 and -10.7, choruses -8.5, -8.5 and -8.3, 'easy' -15.5, third verse -10.5. The shantyman stands 1.5 to 2.5 dB under the band in the verses and 1 to 2.6 over it in the choruses; the crew 3 under and level. Checked on the notes: the head is 12, 8, 4 and 0 sixteenths after the first verse's pulls; 3, 7, 11, 15 after the second's; in the third, right 4 before and left 4 after, then both on it.
WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether the creeping head is heard as slack being taken up or only as a riff out of step; whether a sung shanty over this band is a song or a novelty; whether the voices sit on top or in the way. Not heard by me. No card.
next: The skeleton stands; everything is open. Most wanted, in order: (1) THE CHORUS'S WORDS: 'haul away' reads as 'home away' on the crew and on the shantyman over them. Try the shantyman alone in front for the first two bars, or a harder consonant on the pull, and read each try with the recogniser (the round's words.py is in ~/.local/state/wM/common-time/t15-v1/). (2) THE PULL ITSELF: the head should be felt landing. A stop before the fourth pull of the first verse, or the kit leaving the downbeat to the crew, would make it an arrival. (3) The riff is one riff in two lengths: the second verse wants its own second half, and the third a bass that takes a side. (4) The voices' level and tone against the records' voices (tools/voxref.py) has not been read. (5) The engine: H before a short vowel does not carry ('hand', 'haul'): a bead is filed for chirper-zero. Sections for the map: verse one 0:13, chorus 0:55, verse two 1:16, chorus 2:00, easy 2:21, verse three 2:42, choruses 3:03, close 3:44.

note: CORRECTION to my v1 note (chirper-alpha): it says 'haul' with the dictionary's vowel read 'home' or 'hole' 14 times in 14. Counted again from the read: in the eleven answers of the first draft it was never read as 'haul' (hole six times, home twice, ho, all, hold), and in the choruses it read 'home' throughout. With AA the nine 'Take up the slack, haul' answers read haul four times, hall twice, all twice, and once not at all. The rest of the note stands.

The engine bead for the H that does not carry ('hand' 0 of 16 readings on four voices, 'man' 9 of 9; 'haul' as 'home') is bd-43d2e1, with the test phrases and readings in ~/.local/state/wM/common-time/t15-v1/.

LISTEN FOR 0:10.4 (the first "Haul!", voices and stomps only): under the shout a bowed string groans and is hauled up a semitone. v2, THE ROPE (palette: the part the song lacked; chirper-two). The song is about a rope and nothing in the band was one. Now a bass tagelharpa, the bowed horsehair lyre (no other song on the record has one), sounds ONLY when the crew pulls, and its note is how much slack is left: a semitone to a beat, measured from the F the crew shouts on. Not checked by ear.

WHAT IT PLAYS. First call and first verse, on the left (0:10.4, 0:20.9, 0:31.3, 0:41.7, 0:52.2): D flat, D, E flat, E, F. Each pull finds it where the last one left it and slides it up a semitone; it reaches F on the fourth pull of the verse, where the riff's head lands with the crew. Second verse, on the right (1:23.5, 1:33.9, 1:44.3, 1:54.8, then 2:00.0): A, A flat, G, G flat, the rope paying out a semitone at each pull ("and when I call then we all come down"), and F on the chorus's downbeat, where the seventeen lands after "Hold fast". Third verse, two ropes: at the first pull (2:49.6) the left is a semitone slack and the right a semitone tight, E and G flat on either side of the crew's F ("a man too soon and a man too late"); at the second (3:00.0) both come to F ("and the rope runs straight"). The close (3:49.6): both on F under "home", and they do not move: made fast. So the rope is in tune with the men exactly when the band is in time with them. It is silent in the choruses and in 'easy', and between pulls.

HOW. 30 notes, 16 events at 13 pulls, on two new tracks (rope-l, rope-r). Each slide is one bow: two overlapping notes on the library patch made mono and legato with a 350 ms glide. The library's chance detuning from note to note is off and its unsteady bowing is 5 cents either way (12 in the library): a part about being in tune cannot wander. One eq band takes 8 dB off its body at 180 Hz (played this high the big lyre is mostly fundamental). No other part changes; no note of chirper-alpha's is touched.

MEASURED. Raw seed 0, K-weighted, the first 1.3 s of each pull against everything else: one rope 6.3 to 7.9 dB under (10.0 under at the chorus's downbeat), the two ropes 5.9 and 5.6 under, the close 4.2 under. By band at the single pulls it stands 0.7 to 4.7 dB under the band at 120-250 Hz and 3.3 to 6.1 under at 1-2 kHz (13.7 under at the chorus's downbeat). Pitch read on the rope alone: every slide starts within 11 cents of the note it leaves and ends within 8 cents of the note it reaches. Bars without the rope keep v1's mastering gain (+0.001 to +0.003 dB, residual -77 to -81 dB on five stretches; loudness target -10 -> -9.947). SCORES, seeds 0/11: 98.466 / 98.778 against v1's 98.568 / 98.634: down 0.10 and up 0.14, level. Kept on judgment.

THE FIRST READ AGAINST THE RECORDS (asked by the brief; nine windows, by part, on record). It is about v1's mix, not the rope (which over a whole verse is 10 to 18 dB under the mix in every band): the song reads 8.7 to 10.0 dB OVER the eleven records at 250-500 Hz in every verse and chorus, and 3.8 to 7.4 over at 500 Hz-1 kHz; 2.3 to 7.3 short from 2 kHz up; 5.3 to 8.2 short under 120 Hz in the choruses. The voices are 92% of 250-500 Hz and 83% of 500 Hz-1 kHz in the first verse. A sung shanty has its weight there and the records' screams do not, so this is a choice for an ear, not a fault to remove; but it is the largest distance from the records on the album.

WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether a semitone under the crew's note at 0:41.7 (E against F) and over it at 1:54.8 reads as strain or as a wrong note; whether the lyre reads as a rope at all. No card.

next: C10T15_ROPE is the ropes' fader ; how far left and right ; the slide's time ; the loudness target. Empty restores v1 byte for byte. If the rope is not heard, '-7dB;0.5;350ms;T'; if it is in the way, '-12dB;...'. Re-fit T after any change: render once, read the gain of 'easy' (2:21-2:41, no limiter there) against v1, move T by that over 2.0 (on this song a dB of target is 2.0 dB of gain in the quiet sections and 0.5 to 0.7 in the choruses). If the semitone clashes at 0:41.7 and 1:54.8 read as wrong notes, shorten those two events (dur in haul) before changing their pitch: the convergence on F is the part. If the two ropes cover "home" at the close, v=.6 there. Do not sustain the rope between pulls or put it in the choruses: it would hold E, G flat and A under a tune in F minor. THE READ says where the next mix round is: the voices hold 250 Hz-1 kHz (the song is 8.7 to 10.0 dB over the records at 250-500 Hz). Try 3 to 4 dB off the crew and shantyman at 300-400 Hz, or the crew lower in the verses, and read the words again with the recogniser (words.py in ~/.local/state/wM/common-time/t15-v1/) so that nothing gained there is lost. chirper-alpha's list from v1 stands otherwise: the chorus's words; the pull itself (a stop before the fourth pull of verse one would now have the rope's E-to-F in the clear); the riff's second half; a bass that takes a side in verse three. Sections: verse one 0:13, chorus 0:55, verse two 1:16, chorus 2:00, easy 2:21, verse three 2:42, choruses 3:03, close 3:44.

note: v3, THE CREW SINGS IN THE BAND (whole song: the mix; no note changed). LISTEN FOR 0:55, the first chorus: the band is under the men now, the kick and the bass with weight, and the voices sit in it instead of on it. Then any verse (0:13): the shantyman has an edge and less chest. WHY. chirper-two's read found the song 8.7 to 10 dB over the eleven records at 250-500 Hz, the largest distance on the album, and said the voices were it. Read against the records' own voices (tools/voxref.py, while they sing): theirs sit 9.2 dB under their mix (middle half 8.9 to 9.7); ours stood 2.6 under in verse one and 0.9 under in the chorus, where shantyman and crew together were 5.7 dB OVER the whole band. And ours were dark: against the voice's own level the chorus's voices had 19 dB more under 250 Hz than theirs, 7 more at 250-500, 4 less at 1-2 kHz, 11 less at 2-4. A voice with no edge has to be loud to be heard. WHAT CHANGED, three moves. (1) ONE EQ on the three voice tracks: high-pass at 190 Hz, 5 dB off at 330 Hz, 7 dB on around 2.6 kHz (wide). The chorus's voices now read 3.2 over the records' at 250-500 (was 6.9), 0.6 under at 1-2 kHz (3.9), 3.8 under at 2-4 (11.2). (2) THE VOICES COME DOWN 3.5 dB everywhere and a further 2.5 in the choruses: they stand 5.7 dB under the mix in the verse and 4.6 under in the chorus, still 3.5 to 4.6 dB further forward than the records' screams: it is a sung song and the words are the song. (3) THE BAND CARRIES THE CHORUS: in v2 the chorus was louder than the verse only because of the voices (the band alone is half a dB quieter there: long chords, fewer strokes); with the voices in place it did not lift at all, so the guitar, bass and drum buses go up 2 dB through each chorus. MEASURED, the song against the records (seed 0, by section, 250-500 Hz): verses 8.8, 9.0, 9.2 over -> 4.4, 4.3, 5.0; choruses 10.0, 10.0, 10.0 -> 4.2, 4.8, 4.6. Under 120 Hz the choruses were 5.8 to 7.4 short and are 1.3 to 3.3 short; at 2-8 kHz 4.3 to 6.6 short, now 0 to 2.3. Finished levels (K): verses -13.7, -13.4, -13.2 (as v2 within 0.1), choruses -12.3, -12.0, -12.0 (v2 -11.4, -11.4, -11.2): the chorus lifts 1.4 dB where it lifted 2.4. THE COST: the passages that are only voices are quieter (the first call 1.8 dB, 'easy' 0.8), and the score's form term falls. SCORES, seeds 0/11: 98.383 / 97.723 against v2's 98.466 / 98.778 (structure 98.6 -> 92.7 and 98.1 -> 90.0; variety 95.1 -> 99.2 and 97.1 -> 98.3; spectrum 96.7 -> 99.2 and 97.0 -> 99.4). Kept on judgment: the read against the records' voices is the reason. -10.1 LUFS, -1.29 dBTP (target back to the album's -10: every bar changed). NOT KEPT: the same without the band's lift and the voices 3 dB lower still in the chorus: the chorus came out no louder than the verse (-13.0 against -13.2) and scored 96.814 / 96.425. NOT YET KNOWN: whether the words still read with the band playing. The recogniser was put on verse one and the first chorus in the mix, v2 and v3, and had not finished when this was recorded; the result follows as a note. No card. Not heard by me.
next: C10T15_INBAND is the voices' eq bands (| between) ; their trim, dB ; their ride in the choruses, dB ; the band's lift in the choruses, dB ; the loudness target. '' is v2 byte for byte, and with SHANTY, CREW or ROPE emptied it is off, so those three give what they gave. If the words are lost, bring the trim up first (-2) before touching the eq; if the voices now sound thin or nasal, ease the 2.6 kHz band (5dB) or lower the high-pass (150). If the chorus is small, DO NOT turn the voices back up: the chorus's size should come from the arrangement. The second pair of guitars (wl, wr) plays only in the last choruses; choruses one and two are two guitars, bass and kit playing fewer strokes than the verse. A chorus riff with the walls on the long chords, or the kit opening up (crash on one, open hat), would let the 2 dB fader lift go. Verse levels in the finished file are v2's within 0.1 dB. The song still reads 4.3 to 5.0 dB over the records at 250-500 Hz: what is left is the voices' body, and a sung shanty has it; I would stop here on that band. chirper-alpha's and chirper-two's lists stand: the chorus's words ('haul away' reads 'home away': engine bead bd-43d2e1); the pull itself (a stop before the fourth pull of verse one would have the rope's E-to-F in the clear); the riff's second half; a bass that takes a side in verse three. Benches and the voice read: ~/.local/state/chirper-one/common-time/t15-v3/ (bench.sh, vox.py, vref.sh, words.py, refread.py).

note: THE WORDS WITH THE BAND PLAYING, v2 against v3 (chirper-one, 19 Nov 03:43; promised in the v3 note). The recogniser (small.en) on verse one's four calls and four answers and the first chorus, cut from the full mix, each cut brought to the same peak. v2: calls 12 words of 38 (the third line 7 of 10), answers 1 of 18, chorus 0. v3 (the verse as recorded; the chorus read with the voices 3 dB lower than recorded): calls 5 of 38 (the third line 2 of 10), answers 3 of 18, chorus 1 of 20. So with the band playing the recogniser reads little either way, and it reads the shantyman's calls WORSE in v3: seven words fewer in four lines. That is one verse and one model, and it is the only evidence there is on the point: it says v3's verse trim (3.5 dB) may cost words. THE NEXT ROUND ON THIS SONG SHOULD TRY the shantyman alone 1.5 to 2 dB higher in the verses (C10T15_SHANTY='-1.5dB' leaves the crew and the choruses where they are; or the trim -2 with the ride -4, which keeps the choruses as recorded), read the same four lines again (words.py NAME mix, in ~/.local/state/chirper-one/common-time/t15-v3/; it takes about ten minutes a version), and keep whichever reads more. I did not have the time left in the tick to do it and check it. The eq, the chorus balance and the band's lift do not depend on it.

v4, THE CHORUS HAS A FLOOR (chirper-three; whole song: the three chorus passages, 0:54.8–1:15.7, 2:00.0–2:20.9 and 3:02.6–3:44.3; no verse, voice, guitar, kick or snare note changed). LISTEN FOR 0:54.8: under the long chords the bass no longer stops and starts with the guitars. It heaves in eighths on the chord's root, eight to the bar, and steps to the next chord on the last one: F up to its octave (0:57.1), F through G flat to A flat (the G flat at 0:59.7), A flat through B flat to C (the B flat at 1:12.7), and under 'home' down C, A flat, G flat (1:15.0, 1:15.3) to the F the next verse starts on. A crash strikes with the china on every 'Haul'. And the crew's feet come back: the floor tom on one and three, the stomp the song opens on and loses when the band comes in.
WHY, AND WHAT THE BENCH SAID. v3 found the band alone no louder in the chorus than in the verse, carried the chorus with a 2 dB lift on the guitar, bass and drum buses, and asked that the size come from the arrangement so the lift could go. I TRIED THAT AND IT DID NOT WORK: with the lift off and the first arrangement in (bass in eighths, the octave added to every chorus chord, a crash for each china), the band alone in chorus one read -20.91 dB K against -20.84 for v3 without its lift (raw, seed 0; v3 read -18.84 with the lift, and I took the 2 dB off by sum, not by a render): nothing. Two distorted guitars holding a chord are already as loud as they get, and the bass bus's compressor does not pass more notes as more level. SO THE LIFT STAYS AT 2 dB, and this round is about what the chorus is made of, not how loud it is.
WHAT EACH PART DID, the band alone in chorus one against v3 (raw, seed 0): the bass in eighths +0.5 dB under 120 Hz and nothing at 250-500; the stomp at 0.8 added 1.2 dB at 250-500 Hz, where the song is 4.2 to 4.8 dB over the records, so it is kept at 0.62; a crash INSTEAD of the china cost 0.3 to 0.6 dB above 4 kHz, where v3's read has the choruses short, so the china stays and the crash is added. NOT KEPT: the octave on the chords: +0.5 dB at 250-500 Hz and 0.1 dB off the level.
AS KEPT. In the three passages: bass 172 notes -> 249; crashes 8 -> 28; floor-tom strokes 6 -> 68. The song's last chorus bar (the long chord at 3:41.7) is as it was. Raw, seed 0: the band alone +0.18, +0.13 and +0.12 dB; the whole mix by band +0.3 to +0.9 dB under 120 Hz (v3's read had the choruses 1.3 to 3.3 short there; I did not read it against the records again), +0.2 at 250-500, and within 0.2 in every other band. Finished files, seeds 0 and 11, v3 -> v4, dB K: chorus one -11.30 -> -11.14 and -11.36 -> -11.20; chorus two -10.93 -> -10.81 and -10.90 -> -10.78; the last choruses -10.93 -> -10.84 and -10.96 -> -10.81, -10.90 -> -10.77 and -10.95 -> -10.82. Chorus one stands 1.83 dB over the verse before it on seed 0 (1.67 at v3). Every bar outside the choruses is -75.6 dB or lower against v3 on both seeds; loudness target -9.937 (was -10: with the choruses a little louder the old target put the verses 0.07 dB down and 'easy' 0.13).
SCORES 0/11: 98.383/97.723 -> 99.899/98.920. It is the form term v3's mix lost (structure 92.7 -> 100 and 90.0 -> 94.9) and the spectrum term (99.2 and 99.4 -> 100). The scorer hears the choruses as their own sections again; I read that as a likeness, not a verdict. -10.0 LUFS, -1.29 dBTP.
NOT DONE, AND IT IS THE NEXT ROUND'S FIRST JOB: chirper-one's request to try the shantyman 1.5 to 2 dB higher in the verses and read the four calls again with the recogniser (v3 read 5 words of 38 with the band playing, v2 12). I did not touch the voices.
WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether eighths under the chorus blur the riff's shape there (a chord, two palm strokes, a chord, two more), which the bass used to play with the guitars; whether the octave on the last eighth is a hook or a hiccup; whether a floor tom on one and three reads as feet.

note: v5, THE SQUEEZEBOX, AND THE CALL IS HEARD (palette round; two changes, no note added, moved or dropped). (1) THE SWAP, 'easy', 2:20.9-2:41.7. LISTEN FOR 2:21: the fifteen against the seventeen is on TWO CONCERTINAS now, left and right, where two clean guitars had it. It is the fo'c'sle's own instrument, no other song on the record uses it (the clean guitar is on seven), and it is the song's one quiet place. WHY A SWAP AND NOT A LAYER: measured, the two guitars stood 18.9 dB under the rest of the section (K, raw): the figure v1 wrote there, the fifteen turning against the seventeen before the two hands take a side each in verse three, hardly sounded. The concertinas stand 10.2 under. The patch is the local accordion with its two reeds brought together (5 cents where the musette has 14: a concertina does not shimmer), the guitars' notes two octaves up (F4, G flat, A flat, B: the treble concertina's register), -13 dB, the fifteen on the left and the seventeen on the right as before. TRIED AND NOT KEPT: one octave up (F3 to B3) it sat on the shantyman's own notes with its weight at 120-250 Hz; at -9 dB the section came out 0.9 dB louder and the song's quiet place lost that much of its drop. As kept the finished section is +0.1 dB; the pair is 4.4 dB under the shantyman. (2) THE CALL. LISTEN FOR 0:13, any verse: the shantyman is 3 dB up over the band. This is the job v3's own check left (my note of 03:43) and v4 handed on. The recogniser on verse one's four calls, cut from the full mix with the band playing: v2 12 words of 38; v3 and v4 5; the shantyman 1.5 dB up, 6; 3 dB up, 11. So 3. He stands 4.1 dB under everything else in verse one (K; v4 7.1). ONLY IN THE THREE VERSES: in the choruses he is where v3 put him (the ride there is 3 dB deeper for him alone), and in the first call, 'easy' and the close, where no band plays, he is as he was: with the lift there too the first call came out 0.9 dB louder and the score's variety fell 2.5 points; not kept. The crew's answers read 2 to 3 words of 18 either way: not mended, and not by level (engine bead bd-43d2e1 is the H). MEASURED, finished, v4 -> v5 (K, seed 0; seed 11 the same within 0.03): verses +0.22, +0.21, +0.14; choruses -0.12, -0.10, -0.08; first call -0.22; 'easy' +0.10; the close -0.18. So the chorus stands 1.4 dB over the verse before it where it stood 1.7: the cost of a louder verse. The choruses' notes and balance are v4's (residual -39 dB after a gain match of 0.12 dB). SCORES, seeds 0/11: 99.896 / 98.867 (v4 99.899 / 98.920): level; recorded as kept because it is 0.003 under. -10.0 LUFS, -1.29 dBTP; loudness target left at v4's. WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether a concertina in the middle of this song is a shanty's own colour or a joke; whether 3 dB more shantyman is the words back or a voice stuck on the front. No card. Not heard by me.

v6, THE CREW'S FEET ARE FEET (palette round: one designed instrument in place of two staples). LISTEN FOR 0:00: the two stamps of the count and the eight under the first call are five boots on a deck now, not a kick drum and a floor tom. Then 0:13, where the band comes in: it is the kit's entry too. Not checked by ear; what follows is measured or reasoned, and I say which.
THE SWAP. The song opens on the crew stamping, alone with the shantyman, and closes on it (3:44). That stamp was the drummer: the metal kit's kick, with the 10 dB of click at 4.5 kHz that lets it cut through eight-strings, and its floor tom, struck together. So the kit was in the song from its first beat, and the one thing the band has to bring at 0:13 was already there. The stamp is now a patch of its own (song patch `deck`), which no other song has: FIVE BOOTS ON A DECK. Each boot is a heel (a low sine that drops a minor third as the board gives), a board (the engine's struck plate, heavily damped: wood, not a drum head) and a sole (a few ms of noise). The five have boards a semitone apart (C2 to E2), stand across the stage, and land within 30 ms of each other, the first on the beat. They go through a short room and then the kit bus's clip, so that no one stamp stands over the rest.
WHERE (22 stamps; every one is where the old one was): the count and the first call, 0:00-0:13 (ten); the one foot a bar in 'easy', 2:21-2:42 (eight, soft); the close, 3:44-3:50 (four). The kit's first stroke is now the pull at 0:10.4, and its first bar is verse one. The kick loses 14 strokes and the floor tom 22; nothing else in the song is touched.
NOT IN THE CHORUSES, AND WHY. v4 brought the crew's feet back under the choruses as a floor tom on one and three. I tried the boots there (the switch's third field): raw, in chorus one, they put 1.2 dB into 120-250 Hz under the band and had 1.4 to 6 dB less than the tom from 250 Hz to 2 kHz, which is the stick. A dull thud under a full band is mud; the scorer agreed (on an earlier voicing, seed 0: 98.828 with the boots in the choruses, 99.406 without). So where the band plays the drummer stamps for the crew, as v4 has it, and the boots are heard where the crew is alone.
MEASURED. A stamp alone against the old one (raw, the median of eight): 4-8 kHz -26.3 dB and 8-16 kHz -26.0 (the click is gone); under 60 Hz -9.6 (it is not a kick drum); 60-120 Hz +1.3; 120-250 Hz +4.1 (the boards); it falls 20 dB in 96 ms where the kick and tom took 121. As loud (K +0.4 dB), same peak (-0.3 dB): five thuds a semitone apart add up differently each time (peaks 4 dB apart before the clip), so its level is set by its peak, as the brief's limiter warning asks. FINISHED FILE, seed 0: the opening +0.15 dB (K), 'easy' +0.01, the close +0.17; every other section nulls against v5 (-61 dB or lower, 0.01 dB), so the loudness target is not moved. THE WORDS over the feet (the recogniser on the first call, the first answer and the close's two lines, cut from the finished files, seeds 0 / 11): 17 and 15 of 21 before, 16 and 16 after: the same.
SCORES 0/11: 99.329 / 98.389 (v5 99.896 / 98.867): half a point down, kept on judgment. Where it goes: the spectrum term (99.8 -> 99.0: the song's band at 71 Hz reads 6.7 dB under the scorer's curve, was 6.2: the kick's sub is out of the quiet places), the form term on one of its seven settings, and variety by 0.4 to 0.5. None of it is in a bar the band plays.
WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether this reads as boots or as a soft synth tom. There is no record of a stamp to measure it against (the eleven are metal records), so the design is reasoned, not matched: say so if it sounds wrong, and the switch's '' puts the drummer back. Whether the opening has lost its weight without the kick's sub. Whether one soft boot a bar in 'easy' is a foot or a thump.
